title: Studying in Germany: Tuition Fees, Living Costs and Funding
seoTitle: Study in Germany: Tuition, Living Costs and Funding
seoDescription: Check German tuition, semester contributions, living costs and funding before assuming a low-fee programme provides a fully funded place.
intro: Many German public institutions charge little or no tuition for some programmes, but studying still costs money. Check the specific course, semester contribution, living costs and visa funding evidence before making your budget.
description:
Many German public institutions charge little or no tuition for some programmes, but studying still costs money. Check the specific course, semester contribution, living costs and visa funding evidence before making your budget.

Tuition-free does not mean cost-free

Many German public institutions charge no tuition for certain degree programmes. There are exceptions by institution, degree and location, including some programmes in Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria and many private or continuing-education courses. Read the fees page for the exact programme and applicant category.

A semester contribution is separate from tuition. It can support student services, student representation or transport arrangements. Check what the contribution includes and how often you must pay it. Do not describe a course as free while leaving out mandatory charges.

Master's study and doctoral research are different routes

For a master's, check the required previous degree, subject credits, language evidence and application method. Some universities use their own portal; others use an external application service. The route and document requirements are set by the specific course.

For a doctorate, distinguish admission from funding. You might apply for an advertised research job, a structured doctoral programme or an individually supervised project. A funded employment contract, a scholarship and an unfunded admission arrangement have different financial implications.

Make a realistic budget

Add housing, insurance, food, transport, semester contributions and initial moving costs. Research accommodation in the city where you would live. A low tuition bill does not remove the need for savings while you move, wait for your first payment or search for housing.

Applicants who need a visa must also check the accepted financial evidence. A blocked account is one possible route; a recognised scholarship or another accepted arrangement may be relevant. Use the responsible German mission's instructions before choosing a provider or transferring money.

Choose funding before relying on it

Search DAAD and university funding pages, then read the eligibility conditions for each scheme. Check which costs are covered, whether a separate admission application is needed and when funding starts. Do not count an application, nomination or possible future job as confirmed funding.

Keep a simple comparison for every course: tuition, mandatory charges, estimated living costs, funding already awarded and any remaining gap. It will show whether the programme is affordable for your situation without relying on a blanket claim that study in Germany is free.

Separate a low-fee course from a funded place

A programme charging no tuition can still require substantial living support. Before applying, record tuition, semester contributions, insurance and the costs of moving. Then check the exact scholarship or employment offer, if any. A supervisor agreeing to discuss your project is not the same as a funding commitment. Ask whether support is guaranteed, how long it lasts and what the appointment requires. Keep the official visa financial-evidence requirement separate from your personal budget: meeting a minimum requirement does not establish that your preferred city and housing plan are affordable.

Read the fee page for your exact programme

The useful question is not whether Germany is free. It is what this university charges for this programme and applicant category. Search the official programme page and fee regulations together. Record the degree type, intake, study mode and any rule that depends on nationality or previous study. If two pages appear inconsistent, ask the admissions or fees office which one governs your application.

A semester contribution is not the same as tuition. Nor is a doctoral employment salary the same as a scholarship for a master's course. Keeping those distinctions clear prevents an attractive headline from hiding the costs you still need to cover. The DAAD finance guidance is a useful starting point, but the institution determines its own published charges within the applicable rules.

A cost checklist for your shortlist

ItemWhere to verify itHow to use the information
Tuition and exemptionsUniversity fees pageRecord the applicable rate and academic year, including exceptions.
Semester contributionUniversity registration guidanceAdd every payment date to the annual budget.
Housing and utilitiesUniversity housing service and current listingsCompare like-for-like accommodation within commuting distance.
Insurance and residence costsRelevant official guidanceSeparate recurring payments from application or arrival charges.
Financial evidenceResponsible German missionCheck accepted evidence for your residence route before transferring money.

Use actual prices for a city you would consider living in. If you have not chosen housing, make a range and state what each end assumes. A shared room, a studio and a family flat are not interchangeable examples. Do not treat a national student average as a guaranteed budget for a particular city.

Choose a course before choosing a funding slogan

For a master's, compare subject requirements, teaching language and the academic progression you need. An inexpensive course can be a poor choice if it repeats training you already have or does not accept your previous qualification. Check whether the application goes directly to the university or through a named service and follow that route's document instructions.

For doctoral research, start with the research question and supervision arrangement. An advertised job, a structured programme and an individually supervised doctorate can have different application processes. Ask which agreement provides your financial support and whether academic registration is arranged separately. Do not interpret supervisor interest as a funded position.

Plan for the interval before support begins

Suppose a scholarship starts after registration but housing requires a deposit beforehand. You need accessible funds for the gap, even if tuition is low and later maintenance is sufficient. Ask about payment timing and keep travel, deposits and temporary housing in a separate arrival budget. This is a planning example, not an estimate of German prices.

Is every public-university programme tuition-free?

No. Rules differ by programme, institution and location. Check the specific course and your applicant category rather than relying on the university's public status.

Is low tuition a reason to skip scholarship applications?

No. Living costs and mandatory charges remain. Search relevant schemes, check their actual benefits and calculate the remaining gap before deciding how to finance the course.

Official sources and further reading

Requirements and policies should be checked for your programme and application date. Sources checked on 19 October 2026.

  • DAAD: study costs and finances
  • German government: visa for studying

Related guides

  • German Student Visa Blocked Account: Funding Evidence and Practical Steps
  • Finding a DAAD Scholarship: Choose the Right Scheme for Your Degree
  • TV-L E13 PhD Pay in Germany: Contract Percentage, Gross Pay and Benefits
